Adult Clarias agboyiensis typically achieve a maximum standard length of 29 centimeters [Li = 29 centimeters], a comparatively modest size within the genus Clarias, which contains several species exceeding one meter in total length. The relationship between length and body mass in this clarid catfish, derived from a power-law growth curve, indicates that an individual of this ultimate length attains an asymptotic wet weight of approximately 173 grams [Wwi = approximately 173 grams]. This value positions the species among the smaller-bodied members of its lineage, a trait often associated with life in seasonally ephemeral freshwater habitats where rapid maturation and early reproduction are favored over sustained somatic growth. The length-mass allometry observed in C. agboyiensis is consistent with the pattern documented for other West African congeners inhabiting similar floodplain environments.

Sexual maturation in Clarias agboyiensis occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to its ultimate dimensions. The total length at puberty is 11.2 centimeters [Lp = 11.2 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 10.2 grams [Wwp = 10.2 grams] as estimated from the same length-mass power function. This rapid attainment of reproductive capability is a hallmark of an opportunistic life-history strategy, allowing individuals to colonize newly inundated habitats and reproduce before seasonal drying occurs. The shift from immature to mature status at less than forty percent of the maximum length underscores a priority placed on early breeding, a pattern common among small-bodied clarids subject to high adult mortality rates from predation and habitat desiccation.

Under controlled laboratory conditions held at a constant thermal regime of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C], the embryonic development of Clarias agboyiensis proceeds rapidly, with yolk-sac larvae emerging from the chorion after an incubation period of just 1.5 days [ab = just 1.5 days]. This accelerated hatching time is characteristic of tropical clarid catfishes, whose eggs develop quickly in warm, oxygen-rich waters. The neonates, termed prolarvae, initially subsist on endogenous yolk reserves and have a minute wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 1.3 millimeters. This scant initial mass reflects the limited per-offspring investment typical of a batch-spawning species that produces numerous, small eggs to compensate for high early-life mortality in unpredictable floodplain nurseries.

Longevity in Clarias agboyiensis is constrained by its small body size and the pronounced seasonal instability of its typical habitats. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild is estimated at approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a duration that, while modest by vertebrate standards, is notable for a fish of such diminutive adult mass when assessed at a water temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. This lifespan is longer than that of many similarly sized tropical cyprinids, likely reflecting the species' capacity to survive dry periods by burrowing into moist substrate or by exploiting refugia, behaviors that reduce extrinsic mortality rates. Senescence in this species is thought to be gradual, with most individuals surviving only a few reproductive seasons under natural conditions.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the wet season at 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C], each female deposits approximately 98 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 98 eggs per spawning event] and spawns nearly daily, resulting in roughly 365 spawnings per year [F_R_i = roughly 365 spawnings per year]. This exceptionally high annual frequency of reproduction allows individuals to exploit brief windows of favorable aquatic conditions for larval growth and survival, a critical adaptation in habitats where water availability is ephemeral. The combination of moderate clutch size with extreme iteroparity underscores a flexible, high-risk reproductive tactic.
